    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-01159 / USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-01159-0

    FAPD-AI: In an order filed October 30, 2026, Judge Ryan T. Holte of the United States Court of Federal Claims dismissed without prejudice a pro se complaint filed August 10, 2026 for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b) of the Rules of the Court of Federal Claims. The order states that the plaintiff neither paid the filing fee nor submitted a completed in forma pauperis application by the September 21, 2026 deadline set in an August 20, 2026 order. Court mailings to the address listed on the complaint envelope were returned as undeliverable, and the Clerk was directed to enter judgment. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Polk v. USA (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-01604 / USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-01604-0

    FAPD-AI: In an order of dismissal filed October 30, 2026, Judge Armando O. Bonilla of the United States Court of Federal Claims dismissed a pro se complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The court found that, although the United States was named as defendant, the complaint asserted allegations only against individuals, including state and local officials and judicial officers, related to a Harris County, Texas state criminal prosecution, and identified no non-frivolous substantive claim against the United States. The order notes that a related complaint filed in the Southern District of Texas had previously been dismissed. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Gregg v. USA (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-00448 / USCOURTS-cofc-1_26-cv-00448-0

    FAPD-AI: In a Memorandum Opinion and Order filed October 30, 2026, the United States Court of Federal Claims granted the Government's motion to dismiss a pro se complaint by a federal inmate seeking more than $100,000 under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The complaint alleged that United States Marshals Service and Bureau of Prisons personnel lost the plaintiff's hearing aids during a January 2023 transfer and that the Bureau of Prisons refused to replace them. The court held that the Tucker Act excludes tort claims from its jurisdiction and declined to transfer the case to a federal district court because the United States has not waived sovereign immunity for claims arising from alleged negligent loss of inmate property. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-03216 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-03216-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential opinion in No. 26-3216, In re: Wells Fargo COVID Forbearance Settlement Litigation, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the Southern District of Ohio's denial of motions by Kenneth and Kayla Rogers to intervene under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a)(2) and its denial of their request for an evidentiary hearing. The court found that the Rogerses did not meet the substantial legal interest requirement because, under the approved settlement's class definition, they are not class members, and it noted that the settlement had already been approved and payments had begun when intervention was sought. The court did not decide whether the district court abused its discretion in finding the motions timely. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-04018 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-04018-0

    FAPD-AI: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Everest Indemnity Insurance Company, Bearing Insurance Group, and EverSports & Entertainment Insurance in a suit brought by Sinmier, LLC as a mortgagee. Applying Ohio law, the court held that the settlement agreement and deed in lieu of foreclosure extinguished Sinmier's insurable mortgagee interest once the mortgage debt was released. Because each of Sinmier's claims depended on that interest, the court found the claims fail as a matter of law. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-03942 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-03942-0

    FAPD-AI: The Sixth Circuit reversed the Southern District of Ohio's dismissal of the Estate of Elijah Isham's Section 1983 complaint and remanded the case. The district court had treated the complaint as a legal nullity because it was initially filed by the administrator without counsel. The court found no abuse of discretion in the denial of reconsideration, and it addressed under 28 U.S.C. § 1654 whether a pro se filing on behalf of an estate can be cured by later retaining counsel.     FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit affirmed a United States Tax Court decision rejecting the challenges of Scott and Audrey Blum to IRS notices of deficiency for tax years 1999, 2007, and 2010, which disallowed a $78.5 million tax shelter loss and assessed about $22 million in taxes and penalties.     PRESACT · web feed · White House Presidential Actions · publisher-dated 2026-11-03

    FAPD-AI: Dated November 3, 2026, this proclamation by President Donald J. Trump declares that the solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans and are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens, consistent with United States law and the international obligations of the United States. The text recounts that the Artemis II mission carried astronauts around the Moon in April, states that Artemis III is planned for the following summer, and sets a goal of returning to the Moon by 2028. It also references executive orders and directives on human spaceflight and the commercial space industry, and affirms the intent of the United States to lead in space exploration. PRESACT-SEL-02

    FAPD-AI: In a November 2, 2026 order, the Ninth Circuit granted the Government's motion for an immediate administrative stay and a stay pending appeal of a district court temporary restraining order.     Johnson V. Adgar, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-5468 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-5468-0

    FAPD-AI: The Ninth Circuit's November 2, 2026 published opinion in Johnson v. Adgar, filed under No. 25-5468 and consolidated with No. 25-1392, reverses the district court's denial of Officer James Adgar's post-verdict motion for judgment as a matter of law on Kyle Johnson's Fourth Amendment excessive force claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The panel held that Adgar is entitled to qualified immunity because Nelson v. City of Davis was materially distinguishable from the circumstances he faced, while stating that substantial evidence supported a finding that he violated the Fourth Amendment. The opinion remands for recalculation of attorneys' fees, which is deferred pending the court's decision on the Bane Act claim, and a concurrently filed order certifies a question on the Bane Act standard to the California Supreme Court. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:56:22 Eastern time ET
    Johnson V. Adgar, Et AL. (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-25-1392 / USCOURTS-ca9-25-1392-0

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion filed November 2, 2026, the Ninth Circuit held that San Jose Police Officer James Adgar is entitled to qualified immunity on Kyle Johnson's Fourth Amendment excessive force claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and reversed the district court's denial of Adgar's post-verdict motion for judgment as a matter of law on that claim, with Judge Paez dissenting in part. The panel found that substantial evidence supported a finding that Adgar violated the Fourth Amendment by firing a 40mm projectile impact weapon indiscriminately into a crowd, and it concluded that the precedent Nelson v. City of Davis was materially distinguishable. The panel remanded for recalculation of attorneys' fees, directed the district court to defer that recalculation until it decides the Bane Act claim, and in a concurrently filed order certified a question on the Bane Act standard to the California Supreme Court. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-03056 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-03056-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential order dated November 2, 2026, the Seventh Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment for the Department of the Interior and the Fish and Wildlife Service in Robert Aland's Freedom of Information Act suit and remanded for further proceedings. The court held that Aland failed to exhaust administrative remedies for his request to the Fish and Wildlife Service, which it treated as a separate request from the one sent to the Office of the Secretary. It held that Aland constructively exhausted his remedies for the Office of the Secretary request because that office's October 2022 interim letter did not constitute a determination under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(6)(A). USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-03342 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-03342-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential order dated November 2, 2026, the Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Inguran, LLC in Li Men's suit under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act. The court concluded that the record did not support a finding that Inguran terminated Men because of her age or in retaliation for her complaint to human resources, and that the company's stated performance reasons were not shown to be pretextual. The court also noted that it applies the Supreme Court's Muldrow standard, under which a plaintiff must show only some injury to employment terms or conditions, to ADEA discrimination claims, and stated that this standard did not change its outcome. The court concluded that the Department's 2015 Notice of Intent to Offset letter satisfied the notice and opportunity-for-review requirements of 31 U.S.C. § 3716(a).     Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10463 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10463-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion, denied in part and dismissed in part Ji Xing Fung's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals order denying his motion to reopen removal proceedings. The court agreed that the motion was untimely under the 90-day deadline, and found that Fung had not exhausted his argument under 8 C.F.R. section 1003.1(m). It held that it lacks jurisdiction to review the BIA's discretionary decision not to reopen the proceedings sua sponte. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Southern Equipment & Services, LLC v. Windamir Development, Inc., et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10601 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10601-0

    FAPD-AI: In this unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 2, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit considered a subcontractor's Miller Act claim against a general contractor and its surety on a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contract for a blast booth facility at Fort Stewart, Georgia. The court concluded that the subcontractor performed labor within one year before filing suit, held that the claim was timely, and vacated the district court's summary judgment ruling that the statute of limitations barred the claim. The opinion was issued by Circuit Judges Rosenbaum, Grant, and Carnes. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13871 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13871-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion, affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment for The Hertz Corporation in an age discrimination and retaliation suit brought by Steven Epperson under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act and the Florida Civil Rights Act. The opinion addresses whether a written warning issued to Epperson was an adverse employment action, and discusses Muldrow v. City of St. Louis on that standard.     Larry Thomas, Jr. v. Ron James, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13876 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13876-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion, vacated and remanded a Middle District of Georgia order that denied pro se plaintiff Larry Thomas, Jr.'s second motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis in his civil rights action against Thomas County Sheriff officials. The court held that the district court abused its discretion in finding Thomas had not shown financial eligibility, because his affidavits stated he was homeless, unemployed, and without savings or assets. The court also found the district court's frivolousness and sanctions analyses insufficient for appellate review and remanded for further proceedings. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion, affirmed the Middle District of Florida's denial of Shirley Reed's Rule 60(b) motion in her 42 U.S.C. section 1983 suit against Detective T.C. McKenzie and former Sheriff Mike Williams. The court held that a later-filed summary judgment motion does not supersede a pending motion to dismiss, and that the dismissal itself rendered the pending summary judgment motion moot. The court also stated that its Rule 60(b) review does not extend to issues in the underlying judgment. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Airworthiness Directives; MD Helicopters, LLC Helicopters (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-03 / 2026-22373

    official summary: The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 90-19-02, which applies to all MD Helicopters, LLC (type certificate previously held by McDonnell Douglas Helicopter Company) Model 369, 369A, 369D, 369E, 369F, 369FF, 369H, 369HE, 369HM, and 369HS, helicopters, that are equipped with a cargo hook. AD 90-19-02 requires replacing the overrunning clutch assembly and sprag assembly with airworthy parts and repetitively inspecting the sprag assembly, clutch inner and outer races of the overrunning clutch assembly. Since the FAA issued AD 90-19-02, after further analysis the FAA determined that additional helicopter models are affected by this unsafe condition. This proposed AD would expand the applicability and would require removing certain overrunning clutch assemblies and certain overrunning clutch subassemblies from service, installing or replacing parts, and reidentifying certain overrunning clutch assemblies, as applicable.     Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES · FR-2026-11-03 / 2026-22380

    official summary: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or Department) issues this rule to revise the regulation implementing section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (section 504) as it applies to recipients of HHS funding (entitled “Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance,” (“2024 Final Rule”)), published on May 9, 2024. This rule clarifies that the Department interprets the statutory exclusion of “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments” from the terms “individual with a disability” and “disability” set forth in our regulations to encompass “gender dysphoria not resulting from a physical impairment” for purposes of the regulation. This clarification is necessary to resolve ambiguity introduced in the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule and to ensure compliance with the best reading of the governing statute. FR-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:54:16 Eastern time ET
    Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organizations Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Conditions fo… (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES · FR-2026-11-03 / 2026-22381

    official summary: This final rule revises the Conditions for Coverage for Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs) to clarify outstanding procedural questions and provide additional operational flexibility for OPOs to achieve high performance resulting in the successful procurement, distribution, and transplantation of more life-saving organs. This rule revises definitions, revises the designation requirements for OPOs, clarifies when an OPO's service area is open for competition, and updates the process for appeals. We are committed to holding all OPOs accountable for their performance and this final rule does not revise the focus on improving the volume of donors and transplants assessed in the outcome measures or the tier structure used for re-certification and de-certification of OPOs. Model ERJ 190-100 STD, -100 LR, -100 IGW, and -100 ECJ airplanes; and Model ERJ 190-200 STD, -200 LR, and -200 IGW airplanes. AD 2024-17-03 requires revising the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-17-03, the FAA has determined that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations are necessary.     Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-03 / 2026-22383

    official summary: The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-25-09, which applies to certain The Boeing Company Model 757 airplanes. AD 2024-25-09 requires installing new relays and changing certain wire bundles leading to the power transfer unit (PTU) control valve. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-25-09, the FAA determined that the requirements bulletin mandated by AD 2024-25-09 contains errors. In some cases, those errors prevent the actions required by AD 2024-25-09 from being fully accomplished. In other cases, the errors would allow actions that could introduce new hazards affecting the operation and thus the availability of the PTU. This proposed AD would require, depending on the airplane configuration, installing new relays and new connectors, changing certain wire bundles, doing an operational test, and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-02

    119 HR 8347 RH: Reinforcing Underserved, Rural, and Local Healthcare Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8347rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8347, the Reinforcing Underserved, Rural, and Local Healthcare Act (RURAL Healthcare Act), was introduced April 16, 2026, by Mr. Owens and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce, then reported with an amendment on November 2, 2026. The reported text would provide that a qualified locum tenens professional or advanced care practitioner is not considered an employee of the entity receiving temporary services under the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 and the National Labor Relations Act. The bill defines qualified individuals as physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, or certified registered nurse anesthetists providing services for no more than one continuous year at a single site under a written contract stating they will not be treated as employees. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 00:01:16 Eastern time ET
    106 HR 8660 RH: Valuing Employee Stock Today Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8660rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8660, the Valuing Employee Stock Today Act (VEST Act), was introduced May 4, 2026, by Mr. Mackenzie and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce, then reported with an amendment on November 2, 2026. The reported text amends section 7(e)(8) of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to include restricted stock unit programs in the exemption for equity income from the regular rate calculation for overtime, and changes "exercise" to "exercise or acceptance" in subparagraph (C). The amendments would take effect 90 days after enactment, and the bill limits employer liability for certain restricted stock unit grants obtained before the effective date, within a 12-month period under specified conditions, or under a collective bargaining agreement in effect on that date. BILLS-SEL-01
